data.Documented value: We argue that speculators preying on the closing rebalances of leveraged exchange-traded funds (LETFs) contributed to the Korean market's extreme volatility in 2026. An LETF's mandated daily rebalance is sized by the day's return, which generates an upward-sloping demand at market close. In response, rational speculators pre-position, enlarge the fund's order, and liquidate into the demand they have induced. Consistent with this mechanism, Korean stocks tracked by LETFs reverse about 75% of their first-day response to pre-open U.S. news by the next close and oscillate for several days thereafter, a pattern absent in every control group. Our quantification implies that self-reinforcing rebalance raised SK Hynix's annualized volatility from 100.0% to 136.7% over nine weeks and cost its products' predominantly retail holders 17.6% of their initial investment. Dispersing the rebalance across the trading day may backfire, whereas a flexible leverage multiple could help.

data.Documented value: Manufactured State Immigration Emergencies as State Vigilantism

President Trump shattered norms when he declared a national emergency at the U.S.–Mexico border to build a border wall. State governors have now followed that lead in taking up what Justice Jackson, dissenting in Korematsu v. United States (1944), called the “loaded weapon” of emergency—like Trump, in the context of the border. The governors of Texas, Arizona, and Florida have all issued state declarations of emergency based on (1) migration and (2) the Biden administration’s purported failure to engage in immigration enforcement. These state emergency declarations have not been studied or even identified in legal literature as a state mirror to Trump’s federal declaration, even though they are as norms-shattering as the Trump declaration was both facially and in implementation. In justifying the emergency declarations, the governors have used xenophobia and the logic of self-help from international law. In other words, this is state vigilantism: claiming that because the federal government is not using its power to protect states’ residents, the states are unilaterally exercising it themselves under state emergency authority. This state vigilantism is sweeping, extraordinary, and contrary to the Supremacy Clause—particularly in Texas, which has implemented a parallel system of state immigration enforcement and has deployed National Guard soldiers along the border with instructions to force migrants into Mexico. It is also continuous with the erosion of norms begun with Trump’s border wall “emergency.” In addition to the reforms that scholars suggested following Trump’s declaration, to combat state vigilantism, I propose that the federal government not only focus on Supremacy Clause litigation but also exercise its civil rights enforcement authority and that state legislatures and judges limit the scope of state emergency declarations, to exclude policy disagreements with the federal government.

Due to the threat posed by COVID-19, many colleges and universities around the world opted to switch to online courses and smart working to keep their students, professors, and staff safe during the pandemic emergency. Face-to-face classes, including labs and workshops, have been canceled and substituted with online activities. New administrative procedures have also been established to support the emergency remote education. This article analyzes these changes in light of the experiences of three higher education institutions in different countries, namely Latvia, Poland, and Italy. From this analysis, some aspects have emerged that have stimulated a deeper reflection on the use of digital technology in higher education. .

paragraphs: ### Emergency Remote Education and Smart Working at Three European Higher Education Institutions [[S3|International Journal of Web-Based Learning and]] In the face of the global pandemic, many colleges and universities around the world have had to adapt to the new reality of remote education and smart working. This shift has not only been a necessity but also an opportunity to explore the potential of digital technology in higher education. The International Journal of Web-Based Learning and Teaching Technologies provides a detailed analysis of how these changes have been implemented and the experiences of three higher education institutions in different countries. [[S3|International Journal of Web-Based Learning and]] Latvia, Poland, and Italy have each implemented their own unique strategies to ensure the safety and continuity of their educational programs.

In Latvia, the University of Latvia has been using digital tools to facilitate remote learning and smart working. The university has established new administrative procedures to support the emergency remote education, which includes the use of video conferencing platforms and online learning management systems. This has allowed students and professors to continue their studies and engage in discussions in a virtual environment. [[S3|International Journal of Web-Based Learning and]] In Poland, the Jagiellonian University has been using smart working to maintain the quality of education.

The university has introduced a flexible working schedule that allows professors to work from home, thereby reducing the risk of exposure to the virus. Additionally, the university has implemented a system of remote assessments and feedback, which has helped to maintain the academic standards of the institution. [[S3|International Journal of Web-Based Learning and]] In Italy, the University of Padua has been using digital technology to enhance the learning experience. The university has introduced a new platform for online lectures and discussions, which has allowed students to engage with their professors in a more interactive way.

The university has also introduced a system of online tutoring, which has helped to provide additional support to students who may be struggling with the remote learning experience. [[S3|International Journal of Web-Based Learning and]] These changes have not only been beneficial for the students and professors but have also stimulated a deeper reflection on the use of digital technology in higher education. The experiences of these institutions have highlighted the potential of digital technology to enhance the learning experience and provide a safer environment for students and professors alike.

sections.heading: Overwhelmed by Online Money Advice? How to Cut Through the
paragraphs: ### Section 7: Overwhelmed by Online Money Advice? How to Cut Through the Noise and Build a Plan That Actually Fits Your Goals [[S7|Kiplinger]] If you're feeling overwhelmed by the sheer volume of online money advice, you're not alone. The internet is a treasure trove of information, but it can also be a minefield of conflicting advice. Here's how to cut through the noise and build a plan that actually fits your goals.

[[S7|Kiplinger]] #### 1. Identify Your Goals [[S7|Kiplinger]] The first step is to clearly define what you want to achieve with your emergency fund. Are you saving for a down payment on a house, a new car, or simply to cover unexpected expenses? Once you know your goals, you can tailor your plan to fit your needs.

[[S7|Kiplinger]] #### 2. Set a Budget [[S7|Kiplinger]] Next, create a budget that includes your emergency fund. This means setting aside a portion of your income each month, ideally 3-6 months' worth of living expenses. This will provide a safety net in case of unexpected expenses or job loss.

[[S7|Kiplinger]] #### 3. Choose the Right Tools [[S7|Kiplinger]] There are several ways to build an emergency fund, but the most effective method is to use a high-yield savings account or a simple interest-bearing savings account. These accounts offer higher interest rates than regular savings accounts, allowing you to earn more interest on your money. [[S7|Kiplinger]] #### 4.

Automate Your Savings [[S7|Kiplinger]] Automating your savings is one of the best ways to ensure that you consistently save for your emergency fund. Set up automatic transfers from your checking account to your savings account each payday. This way, you won't have to think about it, and you'll be more likely to stick to your plan. [[S7|Kiplinger]] #### 5.

Stay Consistent [[S7|Kiplinger]] Building an emergency fund takes time and discipline. Stick to your plan and avoid dipping into your savings for non-emergencies. If you need to use your emergency fund, it's best to do so gradually over time, rather than dipping into it all at once. [[S7|Kiplinger]] #### 6.

Monitor and Adjust [[S7|Kiplinger]] Finally, it's important to monitor your progress and adjust your plan as needed. If your financial situation changes, you may need to adjust your emergency fund strategy. For example, if you get a raise or a promotion, you may be able to increase your savings rate.

sections.heading: What is an ETF?
paragraphs: ### What is an ETF? [[S1|Bing web evidence]] Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are a type of investment vehicle that allows investors to diversify their portfolios by purchasing a basket of securities, such as stocks or bonds, without owning each individual security. ETFs are traded on stock exchanges, just like individual stocks, and can be bought and sold throughout the day, unlike mutual funds, which are typically bought and sold at the end of the trading day. [[S1|Bing web evidence]] ETFs are popular with investors because they offer a simple way to buy a diversified investment.

Many ETFs are designed around a specific strategy, theme, or exposure, such as a broad market index or a specific sector. This allows investors to gain exposure to a particular asset class or market without having to individually purchase and hold each security within that class. [[S1|Bing web evidence]] ETFs can be categorized into several types, including index ETFs, which track specific market indices, and actively managed ETFs, which are managed by professional fund managers. Index ETFs are often considered to be the most popular type of ETF, as they provide a simple way to gain exposure to a diversified portfolio of securities.

[[S1|Bing web evidence]] ETFs have become increasingly popular in recent years, partly due to their ability to provide diversification and lower costs compared to mutual funds. They also offer investors the flexibility to add or remove securities from their portfolio as needed, without having to sell and re-purchase the securities. [[S1|Bing web evidence]] ETFs can be a useful tool for building an emergency fund, as they offer diversification and low costs. By investing in a diversified portfolio of ETFs, investors can reduce the risk of losing their entire investment in a single security, which can be especially important for those looking to build an emergency fund.

sections.heading: Swimming with Sharks: Can Small Investors Compete with Buffett?
paragraphs: ### Swimming with Sharks: Can Small Investors Compete with Buffett? [[S3|Preprints org]] Millions of small investors fare poorly in the financial markets. For them, the markets are like turbulent seas. Braving them in a mere skiff, a major storm can spell financial doom at any time.

But the reality is that most investment funds also underperform the market. Against this backdrop, there are some savvy investors who have consistently beaten the market, for decades! Names such Benjamin Graham, John Templeton, Peter Lynch, or Jim Simons come to mind. But no investor has beat the market as decisively or for as long as Warren Buffett, getting an annual return of nearly 20% since 1965!

[[S3|Preprints org]] Is there a way that the small investor can swim with these sharks? [[S3|Preprints org]] These legendary investors developed a refined sense for valuing companies through fundamental analysis (hard work), investing in solid companies that are deep in value. The untrained small investor cannot hope to replicate their method. To enter these waters, she needs a new boat: algorithmic trading.

Not the kind that trades in microseconds (high frequency trading), which is again out of her reach, but the type that trades only a few times a year (very low frequency). Using an approach developed and tested in previous papers, we go head-to-head with Buffett's famous BRK-A fund and compare performance over the 44-year period 1980-2024. Buffett's BRK-A earned 19% annual return over the 44 years. We also test a 50-year period, the historical limit for Nasdaq.

[[S3|Preprints org]] By using simple algorithmic trading methods, we show that the small investor can indeed keep pace with Buffett, without the hard work. Our simple methods allow us to obtain both strong gains, and reduced drawdowns, helping us to survive the major market downturns known as Black Swan events. This win-win is good news for small investors worldwide. [[S3|Preprints org]] ### Swimming with Sharks: Can Small Investors Compete with Buffett?
